extracted.intended_audience: writers, literary critics, and educated readers interested in literary style and criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for producing and judging short epigrammatic maxims, salon-produced literature, and popular pulpit/essay prose — covering form (terseness, finish), originality, use of ornament, honesty of statement, and the role of revision and critique. Includes critique of pulpit-journalistic writing practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sententious/epigrammatic form
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce generalizations to their briefest form of expression, to give them the epigrammatic turn which made them portable in the memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was the specialty of Madame de Sablé’s circle; maxims should be concise, memorable, and strikingly phrased so they travel easily in conversation and memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terseness and finish through remodelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Thoughts should be remodelled again and again to bring them to the highest degree of terseness and finish, like stones cut into facets and polished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal’s Pensées show repeated revision to achieve this finish; material gathered as raw quarry should be reworked, not merely collected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal perfection vs substantive universality
rubrics_metrics.description: Form may be perfect while matter is true only in certain conditions and false if taken as universal — beware overgeneralization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: La Rochefoucauld’s maxims are 'perfect' in form but often 'true as applied to that condition of human nature in which the selfish instincts are still dominant, false if taken as a representation of all the elements and possibilities of human nature.' Authors should qualify sweeping statements or avoid presenting local truths as universal laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / stamp of individual character
rubrics_metrics.description: Maxims and short pieces should carry a stamp of genius or individual character rather than merely good sense or nobility of feeling without individuality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Madame de Sablé’s maxims had excellent sense but 'no stamp of genius'; aim for distinctive voice or insight rather than only genteel commonplaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the encourager/editor (salon culture)
rubrics_metrics.description: One valuable literary role is to stimulate others to write — showing sympathy, appreciation, and encouragement that fosters originality in others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Madame de Sablé’s strength was to second a man’s wit with understanding; social contexts (salons) that cultivate appreciation can produce notable work even if the hostess herself is not original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek private criticism and revise before publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should 'feel their way' into print by sending manuscript copies to persons of taste and talent and using their written opinions to improve the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: La Rochefoucauld circulated manuscripts and revised in response to criticism; use private feedback to edit both style and substance prior to public release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage publicity and accept external review
rubrics_metrics.description: Notices and journal statements about a work should accurately state nature and criticisms; authors will sometimes alter notices but public critique matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Madame de Sablé prepared a notice for the Journal des Savants that included adverse opinion; La Rochefoucauld edited it. Fixing discourses in print exposes them to the criticism necessary for public accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth of subject-matter (avoid narrow conversationalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: True womanly culture (and good writing) arises when writers are admitted to a common fund of ideas and common objects of interest with men; avoid narrow, insulated conversazioni.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let 'the whole field of reality be laid open' — encourage writers to address the wider world rather than confined decorative topics, so their distinctive mental qualities can complement broader truth and beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid superficial cleverness and commonplace cleverness
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'commonplace cleverness' that lacks originality, force of thought, striking felicity of presentation, or depth of emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drift from being a voluble retail talker whose language is exuberant but not exact; prefer passages worth extracting as 'beauties' rather than sprawling, unmemorable banality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist ornate tawdriness; prefer precise expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Love of ornament can become tawdry; grandiloquent embellishment should not mask weak thought or obscure practical injunctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: draping a prosaic injunction about choosing a house in extravagant religious imagery. Keep practical advice clear and avoid ornament that disguises emptiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance imaginative paraphrase with close exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: While imaginative paraphrase can fill outlines with coloring, writers should avoid inventing undreamed-of details that depart from literal accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dr. Cumming's imaginative paraphrases (e.g., serpent’s speech, Abel’s sacrificial thoughts) exemplify filling gaps with fancy; balance such imagination with fidelity and restraint when exposition demands precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not substitute rhetoric for evidence (avoid wholesale assertion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument that continually slides into wholesale assertion and vague declamation is a flaw; claims should be backed by reasoned evidence, not merely declamatory force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preachers and essayists who invoke sweeping statements without rigorous support produce ephemeral, journalist-like work rather than enduring literature or argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness and intellectual honesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain veracity of statement; avoid 'argumentative white lies' and devices to explain away adverse evidence in service of a doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text links sincere zeal with a danger of intellectual distortion when doctrine is elevated above inquiry; writers should value evidence and the preference for truth as a moral and intellectual habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confirmation bias — seek sufficient evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not select facts merely because they will bear out a doctrine; inquire whether propositions are attested by sufficient evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fettering the mind to foregone conclusions produces sophistic explanations; cultivate open inquiry and weigh direct evidence over congenial but weak supporting facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer depth over 'readiness' in responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Quick 'ready replies' to sceptical arguments may sacrifice accuracy and depth; prefer well-digested solutions when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'Manual of Christian Evidences' aims at readiness for use by Scripture readers and teachers — useful in some contexts, but writers should not make speed the principal virtue at the expense of careful argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix oral work in print to invite scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Ephemeral oral discourse (sermons, lectures) benefits from being published in print because it subjects the work to public criticism and accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preacher has an advantage of immunity in the pulpit; printing sermons opens them to the 'courage and patience' of critics and thus improves public discourse and the writer’s standards.
